newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbs to mark Christmas with 50th day of protest.
newsitem.headline: Serbs to mark Christmas with 50th day of protest.

text.p: Serbian pro-democracy demonstrators plan to mark Orthodox Christmas Eve on Monday with their 50th consecutive day of protests against the government's annulment of opposition election victories.

Protest organisers told Sunday's crowd of more than 100,000 to gather early on Monday evening in Republic Square and then head to St Sava's cathedral for midnight mass, defying a government ban on marches imposed after clashes on December 24.
Sunday's protest got around the march ban by paralysing central Belgrade with a vast traffic jam of hooting cars, many festooned with balloons and trailing Christmas tree branches.
The Serbian Orthodox Church celebrates Christmas on January 7, according to the old Julian calendar.

"I urge you all to come tomorrow in your cars, which will help us by following a procession headed by our students and clergymen to St Sava's cathedral, where we shall burn a Yule log and Patriarch Pavle will hold the Christmas Eve liturgy," Vuk Draskovic, one of the opposition leaders, told the rally.
He warned that security forces could try to stop the procession.

Former national bank chairman Dragoslav Avramovic, 86, who became a hero to Serbia's opposition after being sacked by the Socialist government last year for pursuing market reforms, turned out to lead Sunday's marchers down one street.

About 70,000 people filed past the state television building, throwing firecrackers at it and shouting "red bandits" and "come out". The station's contemptuous coverage of the protests has angered the opposition.
Thousands of Belgrade university students also staged their nightly rally, banging pots, pans and drums to symbolically drown out the state television evening news.
On Monday, the students plan to go to the offices of army chief of staff Momcilo Perisic and Interior Minister Zoran Sokolovitj, who have not responded to requests for a meeting.
The movement has won unprecedented expressions of support from pillars of the state, including army officers, the Orthodox church and even elements of the police.
Opponents of President Slobodan Milosevic have held daily demonstrations since November 19 against his government's annulment of municipal election wins by the Zajedno (Together) coalition.

The Serbian interior ministry outlawed marches after a December 24 riot between opposition activists and government loyalists but daily protests against election fraud by the Socialists have continued in squares and pedestrian malls.

Western governments led by the United States have told Milosevic there will be no financial aid to rebuild Yugoslavia's disintegrating economy unless Zajedno's election wins are reinstated and broad democratic reforms undertaken.
Zoran Djindjic, a Zajedno leader, told tens of thousands of faithful gathered in Republic Square: "No one in the world has ever managed to hold out this many days in political protest."

Draskovic warned that the opposition would stage traffic blockades across Serbia in coming days unless the government acknowledged the opposition election victories in 15 of the country's 18 largest cities, including Belgrade.

State radio on Sunday criticised the Serbian Orthodox Church for siding with the opposition, saying in a commentary it was taking Serbia back to the situation before the Dayton peace accords on Bosnia, when national survival was under threat.
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe has verified the opposition claims to have won polls in 15 cities.
The government grudgingly admitted last week that Zajedno had won a few of the smaller cities but said that in other districts no party gained a majority or the results needed further study.
Diplomats said the response was so limited and murky that it effectively rebuffed the OSCE team's findings.
